title: Article 2: the right to life
subtitle: The negative duty, lethal force, and the systemic, operational and investigative positive duties
objectives: State the scope of the state's negative duty under Article 2 and the narrow exceptions in Article 2(2)
Apply the 'absolute necessity' test to a use-of-lethal-force scenario
Distinguish the systemic positive duty from the operational positive duty, and state the Osman threshold for the latter
Identify when the investigative (procedural) duty under Article 2 is triggered and what it requires

leadingAuthorities.role: Sets the 'absolute necessity' standard for lethal force and requires the whole operation, including planning and control, to be scrutinised
Establishes the operational positive duty and the real-and-immediate-risk threshold that triggers it

leadingAuthorities.citation: Rabone v Pennine Care NHS Trust [2012] UKSC 2
leadingAuthorities.role: Extends the operational duty to a voluntary psychiatric patient known to be at real and immediate risk of suicide

leadingAuthorities.citation: R (Middleton) v West Somerset Coroner [2004] UKHL 10
leadingAuthorities.role: Establishes that an Article 2 inquest must answer 'how' the deceased came by their death in a way that addresses the central factual issues, not merely 'by what means'

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Article 2 is the lesson where students most often reach for the wrong duty. A fact pattern about a state agent pulling a trigger and a fact pattern about a hospital failing to watch a known suicide risk are governed by entirely different tests — this lesson is about telling them apart under pressure.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've handled the doctrine here before. The test pool leans hard towards fact patterns — expect to be given fragments of a scenario and asked which duty, and which test, actually applies.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Take Parts 1 through 3 slowly before the operational duty lesson lands. The four separate strands of Article 2 (negative duty, systemic duty, operational duty, investigative duty) need to be genuinely separate in your head, not one blurred impression of 'the right to life applies here'.

overview.hook: In March 1988, three IRA members were shot dead by SAS soldiers on a street in Gibraltar. The soldiers genuinely, honestly believed each of the three was about to detonate a car bomb. None of them was. The European Court of Human Rights still had to ask a harder question than whether the soldiers were wrong — it had to ask whether the operation that put them in that street, with those instructions, believing what they believed, had been planned and controlled so as to minimise, to the greatest extent possible, any recourse to lethal force at all. That question — not just 'was the shot justified in the moment' — is the spine of this lesson.

parts.heading: The negative duty and the narrow list in Article 2(2)
parts.voice: sober, precise — establishes the baseline before the hard cases
body: Article 2(1) states the core: 'Everyone's right to life shall be protected by law. No one shall be deprived of his life intentionally save in the execution of a sentence of a court following his conviction of a crime for which this penalty is provided by law.' The UK has since abolished the death penalty entirely, so in practice that clause has no domestic application — the negative duty in the UK context is close to unqualified.

Article 2(2) then lists the only circumstances in which the use of force resulting in death will not contravene the article, where the force used is 'no more than absolutely necessary': in defence of any person from unlawful violence; in order to effect a lawful arrest or to prevent the escape of a person lawfully detained; and in action lawfully taken for the purpose of quelling a riot or insurrection. Read this list the same way you learned to read Article 5(1) in the previous lesson — it is closed and exhaustive, not illustrative. If a killing by a state agent doesn't fit one of these three grounds, no proportionality argument rescues it.

Note the phrase 'absolutely necessary', not merely 'necessary' or 'reasonable'. This is a markedly higher threshold than the ordinary 'necessary in a democratic society' proportionality test used for qualified rights like Article 8. The difference in wording is deliberate, and the case law that follows takes it seriously.

components.citation: European Convention on Human Rights, Article 2(2)
components.text: Deprivation of life shall not be regarded as inflicted in contravention of this Article when it results from the use of force which is no more than absolutely necessary: (a) in defence of any person from unlawful violence; (b) in order to effect a lawful arrest or to prevent the escape of a person lawfully detained; (c) in action lawfully taken for the purpose of quelling a riot or insurrection.
elements: Use of force resulting in death
The force used is no more than absolutely necessary
The purpose falls within one of the three closed grounds (a)-(c)

components.definition: The threshold Article 2(2) sets for lethal force to be lawful — markedly stricter than the ordinary proportionality test used for qualified rights, requiring force to be strictly proportionate to the aim and genuinely unavoidable in the circumstances as honestly, reasonably believed.

interaction.prompt: Is the list of grounds in Article 2(2) permitting lethal force closed and exhaustive, or merely illustrative?
options: Closed and exhaustive — only these three grounds can justify lethal force
Illustrative — courts may recognise further grounds by analogy
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. As with Article 5(1)'s list of permitted detention grounds, Article 2(2) is drafted as a closed list. If the facts don't fit one of the three grounds, the killing cannot be justified under this provision at all.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Reread the structure — Article 2(2), like Article 5(1) in the previous lesson, is a closed list, not an open invitation to reason by analogy. Only defence of a person from unlawful violence, effecting a lawful arrest or preventing escape, or quelling a riot or insurrection will do.

parts.heading: McCann v UK: absolute necessity and the whole operation
parts.voice: case-narrative, handled soberly — the facts are serious and are given no more detail than the legal analysis requires
body: In March 1988, UK authorities had credible intelligence that an IRA active service unit was planning a car bomb attack in Gibraltar. Three IRA members — Daniel McCann, Mairead Farrell and Sean Savage — were placed under surveillance. Soldiers from the Special Air Service were briefed that the suspects were likely to be armed and might detonate a bomb by remote control if challenged. When the soldiers moved to intercept the three, believing (mistakenly, as it turned out) that one of them was reaching for a detonator, they opened fire and killed all three. No bomb was found on any of them at the point of the shooting; a car bomb was later found elsewhere, not remotely detonable in the way the soldiers had been briefed to expect.

The European Court of Human Rights accepted that the individual soldiers, given what they had genuinely and honestly been told and what they perceived in the moment, believed lethal force was necessary to prevent a bomb being detonated — and the Court did not find that their split-second use of force was itself unreasonable on that mistaken but honestly held basis. But the Court refused to stop the inquiry there. It held that Article 2 requires scrutiny of the whole operation — its planning and control, not only the final seconds before the trigger was pulled — and asked whether the operation as planned had been organised so as to minimise, to the greatest extent possible, any recourse to lethal force. On that wider inquiry, the Court found a breach: the authorities could have arrested the suspects earlier, at the border, before they reached the point where a split-second lethal decision became necessary at all, and the failure to plan the operation that way meant the resulting deaths were not 'absolutely necessary' within the meaning of Article 2(2).

This is the single most important structural point in the lethal-force case law: 'absolute necessity' is not tested only at the moment force is used. It is tested across the planning and control of the entire operation that put the individual agent in the position of having to decide. A soldier's honest, reasonable belief in the moment can be entirely genuine and the state can still be in breach, if the operation was planned in a way that made lethal force more likely than it needed to be.

components.court: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber)
components.factsShort: Three IRA suspects believed to be about to detonate a car bomb were shot dead by SAS soldiers in Gibraltar; no detonator was in fact on them at that moment.
components.ratioShort: Article 2's 'absolute necessity' test requires scrutiny of the whole operation — planning and control, not just the final use of force — and asks whether it was organised to minimise recourse to lethal force to the greatest extent possible.

expanded.facts: Acting on intelligence of a planned car bomb attack, UK authorities placed three IRA members under surveillance in Gibraltar and briefed the intercepting soldiers that the suspects were likely armed and might detonate a bomb remotely if challenged. The soldiers, believing one suspect was reaching for a detonator, opened fire and killed all three. No detonator or firearm was found on the bodies; a car bomb was later located elsewhere.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court held that it was 'not persuaded that the killing of the three terrorists constituted the use of force which was no more than absolutely necessary', not because the individual soldiers' beliefs in the moment were unreasonable, but because the authorities' failure to allow for the possibility that their intelligence might be mistaken, and their failure to take steps such as arresting the suspects at the border, contributed to a situation where the fatal shooting became almost inevitable.
expanded.significance: McCann establishes that the 'absolute necessity' inquiry under Article 2(2) is not confined to the moment force is used; it extends to whether the operation as a whole was planned and controlled to minimise recourse to lethal force. This has become the standard framework applied to every subsequent lethal-force case.

interaction.prompt: Armed police, briefed that a suspect is highly likely to be carrying a firearm and to fire on sight, shoot the suspect dead the moment he reaches into his jacket. No firearm is found. The briefing was based on an uncorroborated single source, and officers made no attempt to challenge or contain the suspect before the fatal moment despite having the opportunity to do so. Analyse whether the killing was 'absolutely necessary' under Article 2(2).
factsToOrder: Officers were briefed the suspect was highly likely to be armed and to fire on sight
The briefing rested on a single, uncorroborated source
Officers had the opportunity to challenge or contain the suspect before the fatal moment but did not take it
The individual officers' belief in the moment, on the briefing given, may have been honestly held
No firearm was in fact found on the suspect

scaffolds.support: Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the fatal shooting was 'no more than absolutely necessary' within Article 2(2), applying the McCann framework to the whole operation rather than only the final moment.
modelAnswer.rule: Under McCann v UK, 'absolute necessity' requires scrutiny of the planning and control of the whole operation, asking whether it was organised so as to minimise, to the greatest extent possible, recourse to lethal force — an honest, reasonable belief held by an individual officer in the moment does not by itself satisfy the test if the wider operation was inadequately planned.
modelAnswer.application: The officers' belief in the moment may well have been genuine on the briefing they were given, mirroring the individual soldiers in McCann. But as in McCann, the wider planning is open to serious challenge: relying on a single, uncorroborated source without further verification, and failing to use an available opportunity to challenge or contain the suspect before he reached the point where a split-second lethal decision was required, both suggest the operation was not planned to minimise recourse to lethal force to the greatest extent possible.
modelAnswer.conclusion: On these facts, the killing is unlikely to satisfy 'absolute necessity' — not because the individual officers acted unreasonably in the instant, but because the operation as a whole was not planned or controlled so as to avoid the situation arising, echoing the breach found in McCann.

parts.heading: Osman v UK: the operational duty to protect a specific life
parts.voice: case-narrative, handled soberly and without gratuitous detail
body: Lethal force cases concern the state's own agents killing someone. A separate strand of Article 2 concerns the state's positive duty to protect life from danger posed by others — including private individuals. Osman v UK is the foundational case, and its facts are a tragedy that unfolded over many months before its fatal conclusion.

A teacher developed an unhealthy fixation on a former pupil, Ahmet Osman, and his family. Over an extended period the man's behaviour escalated — he changed his name by deed poll to match the boy's surname, vandalised the family's home, and was reported to the police repeatedly by the school and the family, who were increasingly afraid of what he might do. The police investigated but did not arrest him, and did not take steps that might have prevented what followed: the man eventually shot and killed Ahmet's father and wounded Ahmet himself.

The European Court of Human Rights held that Article 2 can impose a positive obligation on the authorities to take preventive operational measures to protect an individual whose life is at risk from the criminal acts of another — but only where specific conditions are met. The Court set the threshold deliberately high, conscious of the practical difficulties and resource limits of policing: the authorities must have known, or ought to have known, of the existence of a real and immediate risk to the life of an identified individual from the criminal acts of a third party, and must have failed to take measures within the scope of their powers which, judged reasonably, might have been expected to avoid that risk. On the facts, the Court held (narrowly) that this threshold was not crossed — the escalating pattern, viewed as it would have appeared to the police at the time, did not clearly establish that they knew or ought to have known of a real and immediate risk to life specifically, as opposed to a risk of harassment or property damage.

components.factsShort: A former teacher's escalating, reported fixation on a pupil's family culminated in the fatal shooting of the pupil's father, despite repeated prior police contact.
components.ratioShort: Article 2 imposes an operational duty to take preventive measures only where the authorities knew, or ought to have known, of a real and immediate risk to an identified individual's life, and failed to take reasonable measures within their powers to avoid it.

expanded.facts: A teacher developed a fixation on a former pupil and his family, escalating over months to include a formal name change, property damage and repeated contact with police and the school reporting concerning behaviour. The police investigated but made no arrest. The man later shot and killed the pupil's father and injured the pupil.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court held that 'it must be established... that the authorities knew or ought to have known at the time of the existence of a real and immediate risk to the life of an identified individual... from the criminal acts of a third party and that they failed to take measures within the scope of their powers which, judged reasonably, might have been expected to avoid that risk.' It emphasised that this must not impose a disproportionate or impossible burden on the authorities, mindful of the unpredictability of human conduct and the resource choices inherent in policing priorities.
expanded.significance: Osman establishes the operational positive duty under Article 2 and sets its threshold: a real and immediate risk to an identified individual, known or which ought to have been known, combined with a failure to take reasonably available preventive measures. The threshold is deliberately demanding, to avoid converting Article 2 into a general insurance policy against police operational failures.

components.label: The Osman test
points: A real and immediate risk to life (not a generalised or speculative risk)
To an identified individual (not the public at large)
Known, or which ought to have been known, to the authorities at the time
A failure to take measures within the scope of their powers which, judged reasonably, might have been expected to avoid the risk

interaction.prompt: In this extract adapted from Osman v UK, highlight the sentence stating the operational duty test.
interaction.passage: The Court recalls the difficult choices which must be made in terms of priorities and resources in modern policing. It must be established to its satisfaction that the authorities knew or ought to have known at the time of the existence of a real and immediate risk to the life of an identified individual from the criminal acts of a third party and that they failed to take measures within the scope of their powers which, judged reasonably, might have been expected to avoid that risk. The Court does not accept that the applicants have shown that threshold was crossed here.
interaction.ratioSentence: It must be established to its satisfaction that the authorities knew or ought to have known at the time of the existence of a real and immediate risk to the life of an identified individual from the criminal acts of a third party and that they failed to take measures within the scope of their powers which, judged reasonably, might have been expected to avoid that risk.

parts.heading: Rabone: the operational duty extends beyond police and prisons
body: Osman concerned police and a third-party criminal threat. A natural question follows: does the operational duty apply only to detained persons (prisoners, those in state custody) where the state's control over the individual is total, or can it reach further? Rabone v Pennine Care NHS Trust answers that question, and extends the operational duty into a healthcare setting involving a voluntary, not detained, patient.

Melanie Rabone was a voluntary psychiatric inpatient with a recognised, serious risk of suicide. She was granted home leave by her clinical team against the known risk, and took her own life during that leave. Because she was a voluntary patient, not detained under the Mental Health Act, the NHS Trust argued the operational duty could not apply — it argued that duty was reserved for situations of complete state control, such as custody, where the individual has no autonomous choice at all.

The Supreme Court rejected that argument. It held that what matters for the operational duty is not the formal legal status of detention, but whether the state (through its agents, here the clinical team) had assumed responsibility for the individual's safety and had specific knowledge of a real and immediate risk to her life. Melanie's psychiatric team knew of the risk and controlled key decisions — including the decision to grant leave — even though she was legally free to leave the hospital at any time. The Court held the operational duty was owed and had been breached by granting leave in the face of a known, real and immediate suicide risk. Rabone matters because it shows the Osman threshold, once met, can attach to hospitals and voluntary patients just as it attaches to police and known threats to identified individuals — the operational duty is about assumed responsibility and known risk, not about the formal category of custody.

components.caseName: Rabone v Pennine Care NHS Trust
components.factsShort: A voluntary psychiatric inpatient with a known, serious suicide risk was granted home leave by her clinical team and took her own life during that leave.
components.ratioShort: The Osman operational duty can be owed to a voluntary patient, not only a detained one — what matters is the state's assumption of responsibility and specific knowledge of a real and immediate risk to life, not the formal legal status of detention.

expanded.facts: Melanie Rabone was admitted as a voluntary psychiatric patient with a recognised risk of suicide. Her clinical team granted her home leave despite this known risk. She took her own life while on that leave. Her parents brought a claim against the Trust under Article 2, having already recovered damages in negligence, arguing the Trust had additionally breached its human rights obligations.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Supreme Court held that the operational duty could arise notwithstanding that Melanie was a voluntary patient free in principle to discharge herself, because the Trust had assumed responsibility for her care and its clinical team had specific knowledge of a real and immediate risk to her life at the point leave was granted. The formal absence of detention did not preclude the duty.
expanded.significance: Rabone confirms the operational duty is not confined to formal state custody (prisons, police detention). Assumption of responsibility combined with known, real and immediate risk can trigger it in a healthcare setting involving a voluntary patient — a significant extension beyond the custodial paradigm in Osman itself.

interaction.prompt: In which scenario does the Osman/Rabone operational duty more clearly arise?
interaction.scenarioA: A voluntary psychiatric patient with a clinical team fully aware of a specific, current, serious suicide risk is granted unsupervised leave despite that known risk.
interaction.scenarioB: A GP practice serving a large general population has no reason to believe any specific patient is at elevated risk of suicide, and a patient the practice has never flagged later takes their own life.
interaction.explanation: A mirrors Rabone precisely: assumed responsibility plus specific knowledge of a real and immediate risk to an identified individual. B fails the Osman threshold at the first hurdle — there is no known, real and immediate risk to an identified individual, only a generalised population-level possibility, which the operational duty does not reach.

parts.heading: Middleton: the investigative duty and what an inquest must ask
parts.voice: direct — sets up the procedural strand the tests will probe
body: One further duty completes the Article 2 picture, and it is procedural rather than substantive: where a death has occurred in circumstances that engage Article 2 — a death in state custody or detention, or a death where a possible failure by state agents is in issue — the state owes an independent duty to conduct an effective official investigation. This investigative (or procedural) duty exists to hold the substantive duties accountable: a right to life is not properly protected if deaths that may involve state failure are never properly examined.

R (Middleton) v West Somerset Coroner addressed what this means in practice for an inquest into a death in prison custody. Before Middleton, an English inquest jury was traditionally confined to answering 'by what means' the deceased came by their death — a narrow, largely mechanical question (for example: 'by hanging'). The House of Lords held that this narrow formula was not enough to satisfy Article 2's investigative duty where the death engaged the article. Instead, the inquest must be capable of answering the broader question of 'how' — in the sense of 'by what means and in what circumstances' — the deceased came by their death, in a way that addresses the central factual controversy at the heart of the case, such as whether a known risk of suicide in custody was properly managed.

Middleton connects back to Osman and Rabone in a practical way: the investigative duty is often the mechanism by which a systemic or operational failure comes to light at all. A narrow 'by what means' verdict can record that someone died by their own hand in custody without ever engaging with whether the prison authorities knew of a real and immediate risk and failed to act reasonably to prevent it. Middleton insists the inquest process itself must be capable of surfacing that question, not merely recording the immediate mechanical cause of death.

components.title: The four strands of Article 2 duty
components.description: A map of how the four duties covered in this lesson relate to each other.

nodes.label: Negative duty: do not take life intentionally, except within the closed Article 2(2) grounds, tested by absolute necessity (McCann)
Systemic positive duty: put in place adequate laws and regulatory frameworks generally protecting life
Operational positive duty: take reasonable preventive steps for an identified individual facing a known, real and immediate risk (Osman, extended in Rabone)
Investigative (procedural) duty: conduct an effective official investigation where a death engages Article 2, addressing the central factual issues (Middleton)

edges.label: A death raising a negative-duty question triggers investigation
A death raising an operational-duty question also triggers investigation
Systemic failures often surface through investigation

components.textAlternative: Article 2 comprises four related duties: the negative duty not to take life intentionally (subject only to the closed Article 2(2) grounds, tested by absolute necessity per McCann); the systemic positive duty to have adequate protective laws and structures in place generally; the operational positive duty to take reasonable preventive steps to protect an identified individual known to face a real and immediate risk (Osman, extended to voluntary patients in Rabone); and the investigative or procedural duty to conduct an effective official investigation into a death that engages Article 2, addressing the central factual issues (Middleton). Deaths raising negative-duty, operational-duty or systemic-duty questions typically trigger the investigative duty as the mechanism for holding the other duties accountable.

interaction.prompt: A prisoner with a documented history of self-harm dies by suicide in custody. The coroner proposes to confine the inquest jury to answering only 'by what means' — for example, 'by hanging' — without addressing whether the prison's monitoring of the known risk was adequate. Applying Middleton, is this approach sufficient to satisfy Article 2's investigative duty?
options: Yes — 'by what means' has always been the correct scope for an English inquest

No — where the death engages Article 2, the inquest must be capable of addressing 'how' the deceased came by their death in the broader sense, including central factual issues like whether a known risk was properly managed
No — the investigative duty is satisfied only by a full public inquiry, never an inquest
interaction.explanation: Middleton requires an Article 2 inquest to go beyond the narrow, mechanical 'by what means' question and be capable of engaging with the central factual controversy — here, whether the documented, known risk of self-harm was adequately managed in custody.

testPool.prompt: What threshold must lethal force meet under Article 2(2) to be lawful?
testPool.modelAnswer: The force used must be no more than absolutely necessary, and must fall within one of the three closed grounds listed in Article 2(2).

testPool.prompt: Which case established the operational positive duty under Article 2 and its threshold?
options: Osman v UK
McCann v UK

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the closed grounds in Article 2(2) permitting lethal force?
options: Defence of any person from unlawful violence
Effecting a lawful arrest or preventing the escape of a person lawfully detained
Quelling a riot or insurrection
Preventing significant damage to property
testPool.trapExplanation: Property damage, however serious, is not a listed ground in Article 2(2). The list is closed to the protection of persons from unlawful violence, lawful arrest/preventing escape, and quelling a riot or insurrection — nothing else will justify lethal force under this provision.

testPool.prompt: Put these steps in the order a court applying McCann works through them when assessing whether lethal force was 'absolutely necessary'.
items: Establish the individual agent's honest, reasonably held belief at the moment force was used
Examine the planning and control of the operation as a whole, not just the final moment
Ask whether the operation was organised to minimise, to the greatest extent possible, any recourse to lethal force
Conclude whether the killing was 'no more than absolutely necessary' on the whole picture

testPool.prompt: How does 'absolutely necessary' under Article 2(2) differ from the ordinary 'necessary in a democratic society' proportionality test used for qualified rights like Article 8?
options: They are the same test with different wording
'Absolutely necessary' is a markedly stricter threshold, deliberately set higher given what is at stake — the taking of life
'Absolutely necessary' applies only to property offences
testPool.explanation: The drafting choice is deliberate. Article 2(2)'s 'absolutely necessary' standard is stricter than the qualified-rights proportionality formula, reflecting the irreversible severity of what is in issue.

testPool.prompt: In this extract from Osman v UK, highlight the sentence stating the operational duty test.
testPool.passage: The Court is conscious of the difficulties facing the police in modern societies, the unpredictability of human conduct and the operational choices which must be made in terms of priorities and resources. It must be established that the authorities knew or ought to have known at the time of the existence of a real and immediate risk to the life of an identified individual from the criminal acts of a third party and that they failed to take measures within the scope of their powers which, judged reasonably, might have been expected to avoid that risk.
testPool.ratioSentence: It must be established that the authorities knew or ought to have known at the time of the existence of a real and immediate risk to the life of an identified individual from the criminal acts of a third party and that they failed to take measures within the scope of their powers which, judged reasonably, might have been expected to avoid that risk.

testPool.prompt: Police receive a single, vague, uncorroborated tip that an unnamed person somewhere in a large city 'might be planning something violent'. No specific individual is identified. Someone is later killed by a third party unconnected to any police contact. Does the Osman operational duty apply to the police on these facts?
options: Yes — any report of possible violence triggers the operational duty
No — the risk was neither to an identified individual nor real and immediate; a vague, unspecific tip does not meet the Osman threshold
Yes — because the police received a tip at all, they assumed responsibility
testPool.explanation: Osman requires a real and immediate risk to an identified individual, known or which ought to have been known. A vague, unspecific tip about an unidentified person and an unconnected victim falls well short of that threshold.

testPool.prompt: A voluntary hospital patient with no history or clinical indication of self-harm risk is granted routine leave under standard hospital procedure and unexpectedly takes their own life during that leave. Applying Rabone, is the operational duty likely to have been breached?
options: Yes — any death of a patient on leave automatically breaches the operational duty
No — without specific knowledge of a real and immediate risk to this individual, the Osman/Rabone threshold is not met even though the Trust had assumed responsibility for the patient's general care
Yes — because the Trust is always liable for deaths of voluntary patients
testPool.explanation: Rabone extended the operational duty beyond custody, but it did not remove the Osman threshold of specific, known, real and immediate risk. Assumption of responsibility for care in general is not enough on its own — Rabone turned on the clinical team's actual, specific knowledge of a serious suicide risk.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario more closely mirrors the reasoning in McCann v UK, rather than Osman v UK?
testPool.scenarioA: State agents kill a suspect in the field, and the central legal question is whether the operation that put them in that position was planned and controlled to minimise recourse to lethal force.
testPool.scenarioB: A person known to be at serious risk from a third party's escalating threats is later killed, and the central legal question is whether the police knew or ought to have known of a real and immediate risk and failed to take reasonable preventive steps.
testPool.explanation: A is the McCann pattern: state agents' own use of lethal force, tested by scrutiny of the whole operation's planning and control. B is the Osman pattern: a positive duty to protect against a third party's criminal acts, tested by the real-and-immediate-risk threshold.

testPool.prompt: A prisoner dies in custody in circumstances suggesting a possible failure by prison staff to manage a documented risk. Does the investigative duty under Article 2 apply?
options: Yes — a death in state custody engaging a possible state failure triggers the investigative duty
No — the investigative duty only applies to deaths caused directly by lethal force

testPool.prompt: A coroner proposes to hold an inquest into a custodial death confined strictly to the mechanical cause of death, declining to let the jury consider whether prison staff had failed to act on a documented, known risk. Analyse whether this satisfies Article 2's investigative duty.
factsToOrder: The death occurred in state custody, a context engaging Article 2
There is a documented, known risk that staff may have failed to act on
The coroner proposes to confine the inquest to the narrow mechanical cause of death
Middleton requires the inquest to be capable of addressing the central factual controversy, not just 'by what means'

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether confining the inquest to the narrow mechanical cause of death satisfies the Article 2 investigative duty where a documented, known risk and possible staff failure are in issue.
modelAnswer.rule: R (Middleton) v West Somerset Coroner holds that where a death engages Article 2, the inquest must be capable of addressing 'how' the deceased came by their death in the broader sense of 'by what means and in what circumstances', reaching the central factual controversy, not merely the narrow mechanical 'by what means' question.
modelAnswer.application: The death occurred in custody, a paradigm Article 2 context, and there is a documented, known risk raising a real question about whether staff failed to act reasonably. Confining the inquest to the mechanical cause of death would exclude exactly the central factual controversy Middleton requires the process to be capable of reaching — whether the known risk was properly managed.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The coroner's proposed narrow scope does not satisfy the investigative duty; the inquest must be capable of examining whether staff failed to respond adequately to the documented risk.

testPool.prompt: Why did the Court in McCann find a breach of Article 2 despite accepting that the individual soldiers' belief, in the moment, may have been honestly and reasonably held?
options: Because honest belief is legally irrelevant to Article 2 in every respect
Because 'absolute necessity' is assessed across the whole operation's planning and control, and the operation was not organised to minimise recourse to lethal force to the greatest extent possible
Because the soldiers were later found to have lied about what they believed
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to think the breach must mean the soldiers acted unreasonably in the moment, or were dishonest. Neither is right. The breach turned on the planning and control of the operation as a whole — a wider inquiry than the individual agents' state of mind at the point of firing.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that is most directly relevant to whether the Osman operational duty threshold is met.
testPool.scenarioText: A woman reports to police, on three separate occasions over two months, that her former partner has made specific and escalating threats to kill her, naming a date. Police log the reports but take no protective action. She is later killed by him on the date she had reported.
tappableSpans: three separate occasions over two months
specific and escalating threats to kill her, naming a date
police log the reports but take no protective action
killed by him on the date she had reported
testPool.correctSpan: specific and escalating threats to kill her, naming a date
testPool.feedbackCorrect: That's the crux of the Osman threshold: specific, escalating threats naming a date go to whether the risk was real and immediate and to an identified individual — the core factual question the test turns on.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact that speaks most directly to whether the risk was 'real and immediate' and to an 'identified individual' — the two limbs of the Osman threshold — rather than simply to the number of reports or the eventual outcome.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario best illustrates the extension of the operational duty confirmed in Rabone, beyond the custodial context in Osman?
testPool.scenarioA: A detained prisoner with a known risk of self-harm is left unsupervised despite staff awareness of the risk.
testPool.scenarioB: A voluntary hospital patient, free in principle to leave, is granted leave by a clinical team fully aware of a specific, serious, known suicide risk.
testPool.explanation: Rabone's significance lies precisely in extending the operational duty to a non-detained, voluntary patient — showing the duty turns on assumed responsibility and known risk, not on formal custodial status. A illustrates the more conventional custodial paradigm already established well before Rabone.

testPool.prompt: What question must an Article 2 inquest be capable of answering, according to Middleton, beyond the traditional narrow 'by what means' formula?
options: 'How' the deceased came by their death, in the sense of addressing the central factual issues and circumstances
Whether the deceased's family consents to the verdict

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is applying the wrong duty to the wrong fact pattern — reaching for McCann's 'whole operation' scrutiny when the facts actually raise an Osman/Rabone question about a known risk from a third party or from self-harm, or vice versa. Identify which of the four strands (negative, systemic, operational, investigative) is actually in play before applying any test.
